title: Paranormal case still unsolved after family terrorised for years by flying items
excerpt: One of Britain’s most notorious paranormal cases still has no agreed explanation after a Battersea family claimed 12 years of chaos from 1956 to 1968, with flying objects
content:
One of Britain’s most notorious paranormal cases still has no agreed explanation after a Battersea family claimed 12 years of chaos from 1956 to 1968, with flying objects

09:00, 24 Oct 2026

The Battersea Poltergeist is one of Britain’s most infamous paranormal mysteries. It’s a heavily documented case that ran for a staggering 12 years and still has no agreed explanation.

‌

‌

From 1956 to 1968, a working-class family living at 63 Wycliffe Road in Battersea, South London, reported a relentless onslaught of bizarre events that turned their home into a national talking point.

‌

The alleged haunting became so disruptive it was debated in the House of Commons and even investigated on prime-time BBC television - yet nearly seven decades on, people are still arguing over the same question: hoax, hysteria, or something genuinely unexplained? At the centre of the story was 15-year-old Shirley Hitchings, whose life - and the lives of those around her - were disrupted as the disturbances escalated from unsettling noises to physical violence, mysterious fires and “letters from nowhere”.

‌

It began on January 27, 1956, with an ornate silver key, which Shirley found on her bedroom pillow. No one recognised it, and it didn’t fit any lock in the house.

But the moment it appeared, the family said the house changed, the Tape Library explained. Soon came the deafening metallic banging and scratching, echoing through the walls and floors.

The noises were reportedly so loud neighbours were disturbed and police were called out to the address. Then the activity reportedly turned physical.

‌

The case’s most repeated accounts describe objects moving as if hurled by an invisible person; clocks said to float, chairs flung across rooms and kitchen items flying through the air. One incident became legend: a leather glove that allegedly rose from the floor, shot across the living room and slapped Shirley’s father, Wally Hitchings, in the face before dropping back down, as per Hometown Ghost Stories.

The family also claimed the poltergeist brought fire. Blazes reportedly ignited without warning on beds, clothing and furniture.

‌

One particularly severe incident was said to have left Wally hospitalised with serious burns to his arm, according to the BBC. The story also includes claims he was left with strange gouge-like marks, which the family believed were caused by whatever was tormenting them.

‌

As the chaos continued, the Hitchings family began trying to communicate with the entity. Using rapping sounds and alphabet cards, they claimed they could “talk” to it, eventually nicknaming it “Donald”, History Hit reported.

Notes and letters supposedly appeared out of thin air, often addressed to Shirley. In May 1956, the entity produced a handwritten letter containing elaborate French phrases and an extraordinary claim; that “Donald” was actually Louis-Charles, known as Louis XVII of France, the son of Marie Antoinette, insisting he had escaped the French Revolution and later died in exile.

‌

Over time the messages reportedly became even more surreal and domestic. The case file includes claims of bizarre demands, typed notes and even Christmas cards that would seemingly “arrive” inside the home, signed off as “Donald” - and sometimes as “Spooky Willie”, according to Haunting Nights.

‌

The Daily Mail attempted to debunk the phenomenon in 1956 through a reporter, Ronald Maxwell, who claimed Shirley was creating the knocking sounds herself using a supposed “hammer toe” condition. Nevertheless, during an examination aimed at proving the “toe” theory, an unseen force reportedly swept medical instruments and paperwork off a doctor’s desk, scattering them across the room - unnerving the medic so badly the examination was cut short.

After the family was labelled liars, a South London reporter, Joyce Lewis, and her boyfriend Steve - a London police officer - reportedly stayed overnight to expose a hoax. According to accounts, they ended up watching the lights go out and then witnessing blankets ripped away and Shirley seemingly dragged toward the floor, leaving the officer admitting he couldn’t explain what he’d seen.

‌

Joyce’s subsequent article helped reignite public belief. Perhaps the most terrifying claims focused on Shirley herself.

‌

She later described feeling an “icy, magnetic pressure” lifting her body - and said relatives walked into her bedroom to find her floating about six inches above the bed. Her body would allegedly go rigid “like a board”, her back arching as sheets were pulled out from beneath her by an unseen force.

The impact on the family, and on Shirley’s wider life, was said to be devastating. Her grandmother Ethel reportedly suffered a breakdown and later died.

‌

Shirley claimed the disturbances followed her outside the house too - with loud tappings and flying objects allegedly costing her a job at a West End department store. For 12 years, the case rattled on, pulling in police, journalists, sceptics and believers.

‌

In 1968, “Donald” was said to have left a final message: “My work is done, goodbye.” After that, the activity reportedly stopped for good.

The house at 63 Wycliffe Road has since been demolished. As a result, sceptics argue the story was an elaborate hoax that spiralled out of control, and point to claims that later letters matched Shirley’s handwriting.

‌

Others suggest a psychological explanation sometimes proposed in poltergeist cases - Recurrent Spontaneous Psychokinesis (RSPK), where stress in a teenager may manifest as physical disturbances. But believers insist key moments make no sense as trickery, especially when Shirley was under strict observation and outsiders claimed to witness events they couldn’t explain.

‌

People still struggle to explain how heavy objects were said to have flown across rooms - and even slippers appeared to “walk” up the stairs. Just as baffling are the accounts of deafening, rhythmic metallic raps that seemed to come from inside the walls for years on end, as if the house itself was banging back.

Then there are the reports of small fires suddenly starting on beds, clothing and furniture, despite no obvious trace of matches, lighter fluid or electrical faults. The “letters from nowhere” remain one of the strangest elements of all.

‌

Thousands of old-fashioned, sophisticated notes were said to appear around the home, leaving people to wonder who could have physically written them, and how they could seemingly materialise without anyone being caught in the act. Even those convinced it was a hoax hit the same wall: how could a working-class teenager keep up something so elaborate, so destructive and so public for 12 straight years without being caught red-handed by police officers, journalists and investigators?

And if it wasn’t a trick, then why did the extreme activity reportedly fade away and stop completely in 1968 after tormenting the family for more than a decade?
